name: Menstrual Cycle, Hormone and Pelvic-Symptom Support Guidance
purpose: Provide cycle-aware questions, low-risk support options, safety escalation, and clinical follow-up prompts when reproductive or menstrual context is relevant. This is not a diagnostic or treatment engine.

context_options.label: Menstrual cycle / PMS / PMDD symptoms
context_options.description: Use when the person reports an ongoing menstrual cycle or recurring cycle-linked symptoms.

context_options.label: Ovarian / reproductive care
context_options.description: Use when ovarian or reproductive care is relevant, without assuming a cycle, anatomy, fertility, or pregnancy status.

context_options.label: Uterine / pelvic symptoms
context_options.description: Use when bleeding, pelvic pain, or a uterine evaluation is relevant.

context_options.label: Androgen / prostate / testicular context
context_options.description: Use when androgen, prostate, testicular, or related reproductive context is relevant.

context_options.label: Menopause / hormone therapy
context_options.description: Use when menopause or hormone-therapy context is relevant; record the exact product and ingredients.

context_options.label: Pregnancy / postpartum context
context_options.description: Use only when the person supplies this context; DNA does not establish pregnancy or postpartum status.

context_options.label: Not relevant / keep reproductive guidance hidden
context_options.description: Keep cycle and reproductive support hidden until relevant context is supplied.

principles: Cycle timing is phenotype information that must be recorded; a consumer DNA file cannot measure current estrogen, progesterone, allopregnanolone, ovulation, or uterine tissue.

In a natural ovulatory cycle, estradiol and progesterone generally fall during the late-luteal transition before bleeding. Symptoms can reflect sensitivity to hormone change rather than an estrogen spike.

Hormonal contraception can change bleeding and hormone patterns. Identify the exact product and active ingredients before discussing cycle effects; progestin is not the same chemical as endogenous progesterone.

Cyclic irritability, avoidance, anxiety, depression, pain, or bleeding are reasons to organize timing and clinical questions, not reasons to infer PMDD, adenomyosis, endometriosis, or a medication problem from DNA.
When symptoms are present, use sleep, regular meals, hydration, and activity scaled to symptoms as general supportive options; do not present them as genotype-specific treatment.

domains.title: Cycle phase and symptom timing
domains.context: Map the first day of bleeding, symptom onset, symptom offset, and symptom-free days before assigning meaning to a cyclic pattern.
questions: What is day 1 of bleeding, and on which cycle days do irritability, avoidance, anxiety, depression, pain, or physical symptoms begin and end?
Do symptoms improve within a few days after bleeding starts, and are there symptom-free days in the follicular phase?
Has the pattern been recorded prospectively every day across at least two cycles, including symptom-free days?
support_options: Use a simple daily symptom score and bleeding log for at least two cycles; include sleep, major stressors, medication changes, and missed doses as context.

Do not label the late-luteal or menstrual transition an estrogen spike without clinician-directed hormone assessment; the natural-cycle direction is usually a fall in estradiol and progesterone before bleeding.
confirm_with: daily symptom tracking across at least two cycles
clinician review when symptoms impair relationships, work, safety, or daily function
red_flags: severe mood symptoms with loss of functioning
new severe or sudden pelvic pain

domains.title: Premenstrual mood-symptom support
domains.context: PMDD is assessed from a recurring symptom pattern and functional impact, not from one hormone level or SNP.
questions: Which symptoms recur before menses, how intense are they, and do they remit after bleeding begins?
Are symptoms present outside the premenstrual window, or do they represent worsening of an existing mood or anxiety condition?
Do anger, avoidance, depression, or anxiety create safety concerns or major impairment?
support_options: Bring the prospective symptom log to a clinician; it can help separate cyclic symptoms from persistent or overlapping conditions.
Keep supportive routines practical and non-punitive: regular sleep opportunity, regular meals, hydration, and symptom-scaled movement if tolerated.
If thoughts of self-harm or immediate danger occur, use local emergency or crisis support rather than waiting for a DNA interpretation.
confirm_with: prospective daily symptom ratings across at least two cycles

domains.title: Contraceptive and hormone-medication context
domains.context: A DNA file cannot identify a birth-control product, its dose, whether ovulation is suppressed, or whether a person is exposed to estrogen or progestin.
questions: What is the exact product name, active ingredient or ingredients, dose, schedule, and start date?
Is it progestin-only, combined estrogen-plus-progestin, an implant, an injection, an IUD, or another method?
Did the mood, bleeding, pain, or avoidance pattern change after starting, stopping, missing, or switching the product?
support_options: Use the package label or prescribing record when documenting the medication; do not infer its composition from the DNA report.
Discuss benefits, risks, and alternatives with the prescriber or pharmacist; do not start, stop, or change dose from raw DNA or a symptom theory alone.
confirm_with: exact product label or prescribing record
red_flags: possible pregnancy with pain or bleeding
severe new headache, chest pain, shortness of breath, or leg swelling while using a hormonal method
heavy bleeding with dizziness, fainting, or weakness

domains.title: Heavy bleeding, pelvic pain and suspected adenomyosis
domains.context: Adenomyosis is a uterine tissue condition and is not diagnosed or excluded by a consumer SNP file.
questions: How many days does bleeding last, how heavy is it, and are there clots, dizziness, fatigue, or reduced exercise tolerance?
Is pelvic pain worsening, present between periods, or associated with pain during sex or bowel movements?
Has a clinician performed a pelvic examination or ordered imaging?
support_options: Record bleeding duration, approximate severity, pain score, and impact on work or daily activity for the clinical visit.
Ask about CBC and ferritin when bleeding is heavy or prolonged; do not begin iron solely because an HFE or other SNP was found.
Ask whether transvaginal ultrasound is appropriate; MRI may be considered when ultrasound is insufficient or a specialist recommends it.
confirm_with: CBC and ferritin when bleeding is heavy or prolonged
transvaginal ultrasound or MRI when clinically indicated
red_flags: very heavy bleeding with fainting, dizziness, weakness, or shortness of breath
possible pregnancy with pain or bleeding

domains.title: General symptom-day support
domains.context: These are non-genotype-specific options to discuss or try safely while tracking symptoms; they are not a PMDD or adenomyosis treatment plan.
questions: Which basics are realistic during the symptomatic days: sleep opportunity, regular meals, hydration, gentle movement, or a quieter environment?
Are pain medicines, supplements, alcohol, caffeine, or other substances affecting symptoms or interacting with current medicines?
What support does the person want from others when symptoms are intense, and what communication boundary is safe and respectful?
support_options: Scale activity to symptoms and stop for concerning symptoms; DNA does not clear strenuous exercise during bleeding, pain, dizziness, or illness.
Use regular meals and hydration as practical supportive basics rather than restrictive elimination diets or hormone-detox claims.
Write a pre-agreed communication plan for difficult days, while treating safety, coercion, and interpersonal harm as separate concerns from genetics.
confirm_with: clinician review when symptoms are severe or worsening
red_flags: chest pain, fainting, severe shortness of breath, or new neurologic symptoms
suicidal thoughts or inability to remain safe

domains.title: Androgen, prostate and testicular context
domains.context: A DNA report cannot measure testosterone, diagnose hypogonadism, determine fertility, or diagnose prostate or testicular disease.
questions: Is there current testosterone, androgen, prostate, fertility, or other hormone treatment? Record the exact product, active ingredients, dose, schedule, and start date.
Which symptoms or goals are relevant: libido, erectile function, energy, mood, fertility, urinary symptoms, testicular pain/swelling, or another concern?
Has a clinician evaluated symptoms with appropriate examination, laboratory testing, or imaging?
support_options: Track symptoms, sleep, training load, illness, medications, and treatment timing before attributing a change to DNA or hormones.
Discuss hormone or prostate concerns with the appropriate clinician; do not start, stop, or change hormone treatment from raw DNA or an online interpretation.
confirm_with: exact medication label and active ingredients
clinician assessment with laboratory testing or imaging when indicated
repeated early-morning testosterone testing only when a clinician is evaluating suspected deficiency
red_flags: sudden severe testicular or scrotal pain, especially with nausea or vomiting
new testicular lump, marked swelling, fever, or redness
acute urinary retention, blood in urine, or severe pelvic pain

do_not_do: Do not infer menstruation, reproductive anatomy, pregnancy, menopause, or contraceptive use from sex chromosomes or autosomal DNA.
Do not call an estrogen spike, progesterone intolerance, PMDD, adenomyosis, endometriosis, PCOS, infertility, or a psychiatric condition from consumer DNA.
Do not recommend a medication start, stop, or dose change from raw DNA, a reported hormone theory, or a symptom-day communication problem.
Do not use a negative or missing SNP call to rule out adenomyosis or another clinical condition.
Do not present symptom-day support options as cures, genotype-specific prescriptions, or substitutes for urgent care.
